Isaac. The second of the Hebrew Bible's three great patriarchs and the son of Abraham and Sarah. Born to elderly parents as the fulfillment of God's promise, his very existence was miraculous and central to the covenant. Though less prominent in biblical narrative than his father or his son Jacob, Isaac carries the covenant lineage forward and becomes a figure representing obedience, trust, and the transmission of divine promise across generations.

Abraham and Sarah conceived Isaac in their advanced age, fulfilling God's covenant promise of progeny—his name means "he laughs," referencing Sarah's disbelieving laughter when told she would bear a child. He was nearly sacrificed by his father Abraham as a test of faith in a trial known as the binding of Isaac or the Akedah—Abraham raised the knife before an angel intervened, sparing the boy and providing a ram as substitute.

Isaac married Rebekah, a woman chosen through an elaborate betrothal process orchestrated by Abraham's servant, establishing patterns of covenant marriage that recur in biblical genealogy. He fathered Esau and Jacob as twins, continuing the patriarchal line, though Jacob eventually supplanted Esau through deception and cunning. Isaac lived much of his life in the southern Levantine region, settling in Beer-sheba and maintaining wells and herds, a more settled and domestic life than his wandering father. He became blind in his old age, a detail that sets up the famous deception where Jacob impersonates Esau to steal his father's blessing.

The covenant between God and Abraham passed to Isaac, and then to Jacob, making Isaac a crucial link in the chain of promise that Christians later interpret as leading to Jesus.
